title: CAN GOD USE YOUR RECOVERY STORY TO HELP OTHERS?
paragraphs:
CAN GOD USE YOUR RECOVERY STORY TO HELP OTHERS?
Maybe the chapter you keep wishing you could erase is the very place where someone else will discover that Jesus still saves.
There is a strange moment in recovery that nobody talks about enough.
It happens after the worst night.
After the confession.
After the relapse you swore would never happen again.
After the secret came into the light.
After you finally admitted you needed help.
After you started rebuilding what your choices, wounds, addiction, grief, anger, shame, trauma, or sin had torn apart.
You look backward at the wreckage and then forward at the life you are trying to rebuild, and somewhere between those two directions, a question begins whispering:
What am I supposed to do with everything that happened to me?
Maybe you wish you could delete it.
Maybe there are years of your life you would erase without hesitation if God gave you the button.
Maybe there are photographs you cannot look at anymore.
Names you do not like hearing.
Places you avoid driving past.
People you hurt.
People who hurt you.
Promises you broke.
Nights you barely remember.
Things you remember far too clearly.
Maybe your recovery is not dramatic enough for a movie.
Maybe nobody knows you are recovering at all.
You still go to work.
You still smile.
You still answer, “I’m fine.”
You still sit in church.
But there are battles happening inside you that nobody in the room can see.
And perhaps one of the most painful questions you carry is not simply, Can God forgive what happened?
It is this:
Can God possibly use someone with a story like mine?
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not say your darkness was good.
It says Jesus is so good that darkness does not get the final word.
There is an enormous difference.

Christianity never requires us to romanticize addiction, abuse, destructive choices, mental anguish, betrayal, rebellion, or sin. Evil remains evil. Sin remains sin. Consequences can remain painfully real. Some wounds require years of healing. Some relationships may never return to what they were. Forgiveness does not magically erase earthly consequences, and recovery should never become an excuse to minimize the damage we have done or the damage done to us.
But Scripture reveals something breathtaking:
God repeatedly takes people who have been rescued and turns their lives into witnesses to the Rescuer.
Psalm 107:2 says:
“Let the redeemed of the LORD say so, whom He has redeemed from the hand of the enemy.”
The Hebrew begins:
יֹאמְרוּ גְּאוּלֵי יְהוָה
Yōmerū ge'ūlē YHWH.
Literally, the thought is beautifully direct:
Let the redeemed of Yahweh speak.
The Hebrew גְּאוּלֵי — ge'ūlē comes from the language of redemption, of being reclaimed or redeemed.
Notice what Scripture does not say.
Let the people who never struggled speak.
Let the people with spotless histories speak.
Let the people who never fell speak.
No.
Let the redeemed speak.
And redeemed people, by definition, have something from which they needed redemption.
That changes the way you look at your scars.
Your scar is not your Savior.
Your recovery is not your gospel.
Your testimony is not ultimately a story about how strong you became.
Jesus Christ is the center.
Because the Christian testimony is never supposed to end with:
“Look what I accomplished.”
It ends with:
“Look what Christ has done.”
There is perhaps no more disturbing and beautiful example than the man Jesus encountered in Mark 5.
His condition was horrifying.
He lived among tombs.
He was isolated.
Tormented.
Uncontrollable.
People had attempted to restrain him.
His life had become associated with fear, bondage, destruction, and death.
Then Jesus arrived.
And everything changed.
After Christ delivered him, the man wanted to leave with Jesus.
That sounds reasonable.
Leave the place where everyone remembers who you were.
Leave the people who saw you at your worst.
Start somewhere nobody knows your history.
Wouldn't that be easier?
But Jesus gave him another assignment.
“Go home to your own people...and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and what mercy He has shown you.”
Mark 5:19.
Read that again.
Jesus sent him back toward people who knew his story.
Not to glorify his bondage.
Not to build an identity around his demons.
Not to become famous for his darkness.
To tell them about mercy.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because there is a dangerous way to tell a recovery story where the darkness becomes more fascinating than Christ.
We can describe twenty minutes of bondage and give Jesus twenty seconds.
That is not the goal.
Your testimony is not supposed to make people fascinated with the pit.
It should make people hungry for the One who pulled you from it.
Maybe that is why God has not allowed you to forget everything.
Not because He wants you chained to yesterday.
But because healed memory can become ministry.
You remember enough to recognize the look in somebody else's eyes.
You recognize the excuses because you once used them.
You recognize the isolation because you once hid there.
You recognize the sentence, “I'm okay,” because you remember saying it while falling apart.
You know what it feels like to sit in a room full of people and still feel completely alone.
You understand why somebody might relapse.
Why somebody might be afraid to confess.
Why someone might believe God is tired of them.
Why somebody might walk into church convinced everyone else belongs there except them.
And suddenly your scar becomes a doorway into a conversation.
Not because suffering automatically makes anyone wise.
It doesn't.
But suffering surrendered to Christ can produce a tenderness that theories alone cannot manufacture.
Paul wrote that God comforts us in our affliction so that we may be able to comfort others in theirs.
The word repeatedly used in 2 Corinthians 1 is connected to the Greek παράκλησις — paraklēsis: comfort, encouragement, consolation.
God's comfort does not necessarily terminate with the person receiving it.
It can overflow.
You were comforted.
And someday you find yourself sitting beside somebody else in the darkness.
You do not have every answer.
You cannot fix them.
You cannot become their savior.
But you can quietly say:
“I know this place.”
And then something even more important:
“But I also know Who met me here.”
That may be one of the holiest uses of a recovery story.
Not standing on a stage.
Not getting millions of views.
Not publishing a bestselling book.
Sometimes it is simply recognizing somebody who is drowning because you remember what drowning looked like from underwater.
You sit beside them.
You listen.
You pray.
You tell the truth.
You refuse to enable destruction.
You point toward appropriate help when it is needed.
And most importantly, you keep pointing beyond yourself toward Jesus.
Because you learned something in your own recovery:
You are not the Messiah.
And neither is recovery itself.
Jesus is.
Maybe your recovery began with repentance.
Real repentance.
Not merely getting caught.
Not merely feeling embarrassed about consequences.
Not merely crying because everything collapsed.
But finally agreeing with God about your sin and turning toward Christ.

Maybe your story involved something that was done to you rather than something you chose. In that case, repentance is not about assuming guilt that belongs to someone else. Scripture does not require victims to call another person's evil their own sin.
But all of us, wounded and wounders alike, eventually come before the same Christ with our own need for grace.
The cross levels our pride without erasing justice.
At Calvary we discover both how serious sin is and how astonishing God's mercy is.
Jesus did not die because human brokenness was insignificant.
He died because sin is deadly.
And He rose because death does not get the final word.
That is why recovery, from a Christian perspective, must ultimately become bigger than behavior modification.
Sobriety matters.
Counseling can matter.
Accountability matters.
Wise boundaries matter.
Medical and professional treatment can matter.
Making restitution where appropriate matters.
Community matters.
But Christianity offers something deeper than merely becoming a more functional version of ourselves.
It announces reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
Forgiveness.
New life.
A new Master.
A new direction.
A new identity.
Grace does not merely teach you to manage the old prison more comfortably.
Christ opens the door.
And sometimes recovery is messy even after that door opens.
This needs to be said because somebody reading this is ashamed that healing is taking longer than expected.
You thought surrendering to Jesus meant you would never struggle again.
Then temptation came back.
The memories came back.
The cravings came back.
The depression came back.
The anger resurfaced.
The old coping mechanism whispered your name.
And you wondered:
Was any of my transformation real?
Listen.
The existence of a battle does not necessarily mean God has abandoned you.
Sometimes the battle exists precisely because you are no longer peacefully surrendering to what once controlled you.
Recovery can include stumbling.
Sanctification is not always emotionally spectacular.
Sometimes transformation looks like getting up again.
Calling someone before you relapse instead of afterward.
Confessing sooner.
Apologizing without defending yourself.
Deleting the number.
Walking away.
Opening your Bible when you would rather disappear.
Going back to counseling.
Going back to the meeting.
Going back to prayer.
Going back to the people who know how to tell when you are pretending.
Going back to Jesus.
Again.
Again.
Again.
Not because repeated sin is harmless.
But because grace teaches us not to make peace with what Christ died to free us from.
And when another struggling person watches you live that out honestly, something powerful happens.
They realize Christianity is not populated by people who never needed rescue.
It is populated by people who desperately need Christ.
Paul told the Galatian believers:
καταρτίζετε τὸν τοιοῦτον ἐν πνεύματι πραΰτητος
Restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness.
That Greek verb, καταρτίζετε — katartizete, carries the idea of restoring, putting right, mending.
Then Paul continues:
Ἀλλήλων τὰ βάρη βαστάζετε
“Bear one another's burdens.”
Galatians 6:1–2.
That is church.
Not a museum displaying flawless people.
A redeemed family where truth and grace meet.
Where sin can be confronted without sinners being treated as disposable.
Where the wounded are not entertainment.
Where confession does not become gossip.
Where accountability does not become humiliation.
Where mature believers restore gently because they remember they are also capable of temptation.
Imagine if your recovery story helped create that kind of space for one person.
Just one.
Imagine someone sitting alone tonight believing, Nobody would understand.
Then they read your story.
And for the first time in months, they whisper:
“Maybe there is still hope for me.”
Imagine somebody who has not prayed in years reading about the mercy Jesus showed you and quietly saying:
“Jesus...if You still want me, I'm here.”
Imagine someone on the edge of relapse reaching out for help because your honesty reminded them that secrecy is not freedom.
Imagine a husband confessing.
A daughter returning home.
A believer returning to church.
A wounded person finally asking for counseling.
A lukewarm Christian repenting.
A skeptic opening a Gospel.
Not because you were impressive.
Because Christ was visible through the cracks.
That is why the enemy would love to keep you ashamed of everything God wants to redeem.
Shame says:
“Hide the scar.”
Grace says:
“Don't worship the scar. But don't waste it either.”
Shame says:
“If people knew, they would never look at you the same.”
Grace says:
“Tell your story wisely enough that people stop looking primarily at you and start looking at Jesus.”
And wisdom matters.
You do not owe everybody every detail.
Some testimonies require boundaries.
Some details belong in counseling rooms, accountability relationships, marriages, recovery groups, or private conversations rather than social media.
If your story involves another person's trauma, privacy, children, abuse, criminal allegations, or intimate information, loving your neighbor may mean withholding identifying details.
Testimony is not permission to expose somebody else.
And being “vulnerable” is not the same thing as being wise.
You can tell the truth without telling everything.
The question is not:
“How shocking can I make my testimony?”
The question is:
“How clearly can my testimony reveal the mercy of Christ?”
Maybe you are reading this and thinking:
But I'm not fully recovered yet.
Then do not pretend you are.
There is extraordinary power in an unfinished testimony when it is honest.
“I haven't arrived.”
“I still need accountability.”
“I still have difficult days.”
“I am still repairing damage.”
“I still have consequences.”
“I still need grace.”
“But Jesus has not abandoned me.”
That is testimony too.
You do not need to manufacture a triumphant ending God has not written yet.
Sometimes the most truthful sentence you can offer another struggling believer is:
“I'm still fighting, but I'm not fighting alone anymore.”
Not because commenting makes you more spiritual.
Because sometimes bringing one honest sentence into the light is a small refusal to keep hiding.
Let believers reading these words pray for one another.
Let the comments become more than reactions.
Let them become reminders that behind every profile picture is a human soul.
And if Christ has brought you through something you once believed would destroy you, tell us what He taught you. Your testimony does not need to be polished. Give Jesus the glory.
Someone reading beneath you may need precisely that reminder tonight.
This is why sharing matters too.
Not as an algorithm trick.
As mission.
There may be somebody on your Facebook friends list who will never search for a sermon.
They will never type “Christian recovery testimony” into a search bar.
But they might stop because you shared this.
Because they know you.
Because they trust you.
Because something in the title feels painfully familiar.
And perhaps God uses that ordinary click to begin an extraordinary conversation.
Not to glorify Gospel Warrior.
Not to glorify yourself.
Send it privately to someone who may be too ashamed to respond publicly.
And remember:
Your testimony does not declare that you were strong enough to save yourself.
It declares that Jesus Christ is merciful enough to save sinners.
That is the scandal of grace.
Peter denied Jesus.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The Corinthian church contained people with deeply broken histories.
Yet the New Testament repeatedly announces what grace can do with people who belong to Christ.
Not perfection manufactured overnight.
Redemption.
Transformation.
Sanctification.
New allegiance.
New life.
And perhaps the most beautiful part is this:
God does not merely rescue people from something.
He brings them to Himself.
That is the destination.
Not fame.
Not becoming “the recovery person.”
Not building a personal brand around your trauma.
Jesus.
Always Jesus.
Because eventually every testimony reaches the same limit.
Your story cannot die for anyone's sins.
Your tears cannot reconcile anyone to God.
Your recovery cannot grant eternal life.
Your testimony can point.
But only Jesus can save.
So point well.
Point to the cross where the sinless Son of God bore sin.
Point to the empty tomb where death lost its claim.
Point to repentance.
Point to forgiveness.
Point to grace.
Point to the Savior who still receives sinners.
And perhaps today you need to stop thinking about who your story might help and first allow Jesus to deal with you.
Maybe you are not ready to tell your recovery story because recovery has not actually begun.
You are still hiding.
Still lying.
Still protecting the addiction.
Still blaming everybody else.
Still secretly returning to the thing destroying you.
Still convincing yourself you can stop whenever you want.
Maybe nobody knows.
But God knows.
And the invitation of Jesus is not:
“Clean yourself up until you are worthy of Me.”
The invitation is to come.
Repent.
Believe.
Bring the truth into the light.
Ask for help.
Stop protecting what is killing you.
You may discover that surrender feels like losing everything until you realize the thing you are losing was slowly destroying you.
Jesus does not promise that repentance removes every consequence.
He promises something infinitely greater than a consequence-free life.
Himself.
And perhaps years from now you will sit across from somebody whose hands are shaking exactly the way yours once shook.
They will say:
“You don't understand.”
And you will look at them with tears gathering in your eyes.
Not judgment.
Not superiority.
Recognition.
And you will say:
“Maybe more than you know.”
Then you will tell them.
Not every ugly detail.
Not to make yourself the hero.
You will tell them about the night mercy found you.
About the people God used.
About the prayers you could barely pray.
About the days you almost quit.
About the consequences.
About repentance.
About grace.
About Jesus.
And suddenly the chapter you once begged God to erase will be sitting in your hands as evidence that broken people are not beyond the reach of Christ.
That does not make the brokenness beautiful.
Jesus makes redemption beautiful.
Supporting Gospel work should never be treated as purchasing God's favor. You cannot buy blessing, salvation, forgiveness, or spiritual status. Those belong to the grace of God in Christ.
If God has used this ministry to feed you, consider helping us feed someone else.
And comment.
Tell the truth.
“Jesus is still healing me.”
“I'm still fighting.”
“Pray for me.”
“No more hiding.”
Or tell us what Christ has already brought you through.
Somebody may read your comment tonight and realize they are not the only person fighting for another day.
Because perhaps that is the answer to the question we started with.
Can God use your recovery story to help others?
Yes.
But the greatest power in your story will never be how far you fell.
It will never be how dramatically you recovered.
It will never even be how strong you became.
The power is found in the mercy of Jesus Christ.
So don't build an altar to your past.
Don't pretend the wounds never happened either.
Bring the whole story beneath the cross.
Let Christ decide what becomes testimony.
Let wisdom decide what remains private.
Let humility determine how you tell it.
Let Scripture govern what you claim.
Let compassion shape how you treat the person still trapped where you once were.
And let Jesus receive the glory.
Because one day the thing that makes somebody finally believe recovery might be possible may not be seeing a person who was never broken.
It may be meeting someone whose scars quietly testify:
“Jesus met me there too.”
And perhaps the chapter you once begged God to erase will become the page another wounded soul reads before deciding not to give up.
Your scar is not the end of your story—it may become a signpost pointing another broken heart toward the hands of the scarred and risen Christ.
